title: Summary statistics, similarity and nearest neighbors

cards.question: How is a dataset of N data points with M attributes stored as a matrix X?
cards.answer: As an N × M matrix, with one data point per row and one attribute per column.
distractors: As an M × N matrix, with one data point per row.
As an N × M matrix, with one attribute per row.
As an N × N matrix of distances between data points.

cards.question: If A is L × M and B is M × N, what is the size of the product AB?
cards.answer: L × N.
distractors: M × M.
L × M.
N × L.

cards.question: A is 3 × 4 and B is 4 × 5. How is the entry in row 3, column 4 of C = AB computed?
cards.answer: As the sum of the products of row 3 of A with the matching entries of column 4 of B.
distractors: As the product of the entry in row 3, column 4 of A and the entry in row 3, column 4 of B.
As the sum of the products of column 3 of A with row 4 of B.
As the sum of all entries in row 3 of A plus all entries in column 4 of B.

cards.question: What is the transpose of a product of two matrices, (AB)ᵀ?
cards.answer: BᵀAᵀ.
distractors: AᵀBᵀ.
Aᵀ + Bᵀ.
BA.

cards.question: Which identity follows from the transpose rule for products?
cards.answer: (Ax)ᵀy = xᵀAᵀy = xᵀ(Aᵀy).
distractors: (Ax)ᵀy = Axᵀy.
(Ax)ᵀy = yᵀAx only if A is the identity.
(Ax)ᵀy = xᵀAy.

cards.question: What defines the inverse A⁻¹ of a square matrix A?
cards.answer: AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I, where I is the identity matrix.
distractors: A⁻¹ = Aᵀ for every square matrix.
AA⁻¹ = 0, the zero matrix.
A⁻¹ has each entry of A replaced by its reciprocal.

cards.question: What does multiplying a matrix A by the identity matrix I do?
cards.answer: Nothing: IA = A.
distractors: It transposes A.
It inverts A.
It sets all off-diagonal entries of A to zero.

cards.question: The matrix [[1.5, 0], [0, 0.5]] is applied to points via x' = Sx. What kind of transformation is it?
cards.answer: Scaling/stretching: it stretches the x-direction by 1.5 and shrinks the y-direction by 0.5.
distractors: A rotation by an angle θ.
A shear in the x-direction.
A translation of every point.

cards.question: Which matrix performs a shear in the x-direction?
What is the rotation matrix R(θ)?
cards.answer: [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
distractors: [[cos θ, 0], [0, sin θ]].
[[sin θ, cos θ], [cos θ, −sin θ]].

cards.question: When there are many features, why are summary statistics useful compared with plots?
cards.answer: They summarise the data more compactly than graphical methods.
distractors: They show the full distribution of every attribute in more detail.
They remove the need to handle missing values.
They always reveal non-linear relationships that plots cannot.

cards.question: Why does the empirical variance divide by N − 1 rather than N?
cards.answer: The course uses the formula var̂[x] = 1/(N−1) · Σ(xᵢ − μ̂)², which corrects for estimating the mean from the same sample.
distractors: Because one observation is always held out for testing.
Because the first observation is used as a reference point.
Because dividing by N − 1 makes the variance equal to the standard deviation.

cards.question: How is the empirical standard deviation related to the empirical variance?
cards.answer: It is the square root of the empirical variance.
distractors: It is the empirical variance divided by N.
It is the square of the empirical variance.
It is the empirical variance divided by the mean.

cards.question: What is the empirical covariance between attributes x and y?
cards.answer: 1/(N−1) · Σᵢ (xᵢ − μ̂ₓ)(yᵢ − μ̂ᵧ).
distractors: 1/(N−1) · Σᵢ (xᵢ − μ̂ₓ)².
cov̂[x, y] divided by σ̂ₓσ̂ᵧ.
1/N · Σᵢ xᵢyᵢ without subtracting the means.

cards.question: What are the diagonal entries of the empirical covariance matrix Σ̂?
cards.answer: The empirical variances of each individual attribute.
distractors: The correlations between each pair of attributes.
The means of each attribute.
Always equal to 1.

cards.question: In the Iris covariance matrix, the covariance between sepal width and petal length is −0.3. What does the negative sign indicate?
cards.answer: Sepal width tends to be below its mean when petal length is above its mean, and vice versa.
distractors: The two attributes are completely unrelated.
One of the attributes has negative values.
Sepal width has a smaller variance than petal length.

cards.question: How is the empirical correlation computed from the covariance?
cards.answer: cor̂[x, y] = cov̂[x, y] / (σ̂ₓσ̂ᵧ).
distractors: cor̂[x, y] = cov̂[x, y] · σ̂ₓσ̂ᵧ.
cor̂[x, y] = cov̂[x, y] / (μ̂ₓμ̂ᵧ).
cor̂[x, y] = cov̂[x, y] / N.

cards.question: What does a correlation of −1 between two attributes mean?
cards.answer: There is a perfect (decreasing) linear relationship between them.
distractors: There is no relationship between them at all.
There is a perfect non-linear relationship between them.
One attribute is always negative.

cards.question: What is the difference between covariance and correlation?
cards.answer: Correlation is covariance normalised by both standard deviations, so it lies between −1 and 1 and measures the degree of linear relationship.
distractors: Covariance measures linear relationships, while correlation measures any non-linear relationship.
Correlation is covariance multiplied by N − 1.
Covariance is always between −1 and 1, while correlation is unbounded.

cards.question: What do the quartiles of an attribute do?
cards.answer: The three 4-quantiles divide the distribution into four equally probable intervals.
distractors: The four quartiles divide the distribution into four equally wide intervals.
The 99 quartiles divide the distribution into 100 intervals.
The single quartile divides the distribution into two halves.

cards.question: Which of these is the same as the median?
cards.answer: The 2nd quartile and the 50th percentile.
distractors: The 1st quartile and the 25th percentile.
The 3rd quartile and the 75th percentile.
The empirical mean.

cards.question: How is the median found when N is even?
cards.answer: Sort the observations and take the average of the two middle values, x(N/2) and x(N/2+1).
distractors: Sort the observations and take x((N+1)/2).
Take the average of all observations.
Sort the observations and take the smaller of the two middle values.

cards.question: What is the median of the observations 7, 1, 4, 9, 3?
How do similarity and dissimilarity measures differ in interpretation?
cards.answer: A similarity is often between 0 and 1, and higher means more similar; a dissimilarity is at least 0, and lower means more similar.
distractors: Both are between 0 and 1, and higher means more similar for both.
A similarity is at least 0, and lower means more similar; a dissimilarity is between 0 and 1.
A dissimilarity can be negative, and a similarity is always an integer.

cards.question: How can a dissimilarity measure be used for outlier detection?
cards.answer: The observation that is most dissimilar to all other observations is considered an outlier.
distractors: The observation most similar to all others is considered an outlier.
Observations with a dissimilarity of exactly 0 to some other point are outliers.
The observation with the largest attribute values is always the outlier.

cards.question: What does it mean that a vector space is closed under linear combinations?
cards.answer: Any combination a₁x₁ + … + aₙxₙ of vectors in the space, with real scalars aₖ, is also in the same space.
distractors: Vectors in the space can only be added if they are orthogonal.
Multiplying a vector by a scalar always gives a vector of length 1.
Linear combinations of vectors give a scalar rather than a vector.

cards.question: What is the inner product xᵀy of two orthogonal vectors?
distractors: The product of their norms.

cards.question: How is the Euclidean norm of a vector x computed?
cards.answer: ‖x‖₂ = √(Σ xₙ²) = √(xᵀx).
distractors: ‖x‖₂ = Σ |xₙ|.
‖x‖₂ = max |xₙ|.
‖x‖₂ = xxᵀ.

cards.question: How is the squared Frobenius norm of a matrix X computed?
cards.answer: ‖X‖²_F = Σᵢ,ⱼ x²ᵢⱼ = trace(XXᵀ) = trace(XᵀX).
distractors: ‖X‖²_F = Σᵢ x²ᵢᵢ, the sum of the squared diagonal entries only.
‖X‖²_F = trace(X).
‖X‖²_F = the largest absolute entry of X.

cards.question: What does the trace of a square matrix A compute?
cards.answer: The sum of its diagonal elements, Σᵢ aᵢᵢ.
distractors: The product of its diagonal elements.
The sum of all its elements.
The sum of its squared elements.

cards.question: What is the general Minkowski (p-)distance between x and y?
cards.answer: dₚ(x, y) = (Σⱼ |xⱼ − yⱼ|ᵖ)^(1/p) = ‖x − y‖ₚ.
distractors: dₚ(x, y) = Σⱼ |xⱼ − yⱼ|ᵖ, without the 1/p power.
dₚ(x, y) = (Σⱼ |xⱼ|ᵖ)^(1/p) + (Σⱼ |yⱼ|ᵖ)^(1/p).
dₚ(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖ₚ‖y‖ₚ).

cards.question: What is the max-norm distance d∞(x, y)?
cards.answer: The largest absolute difference across attributes, max{|x₁ − y₁|, …, |x_M − y_M|}.
distractors: The sum of the absolute differences across attributes.
The square root of the sum of squared differences.
The smallest absolute difference across attributes.

cards.question: In 2D, what shape is the set of points within distance 1 of the origin under the 1-norm, 2-norm and ∞-norm respectively?
cards.answer: A diamond (rotated square), a circle, and an axis-aligned square.
distractors: A circle, a diamond, and an axis-aligned square.
An axis-aligned square, a circle, and a diamond.
A circle in all three cases.

cards.question: Which p-distance is most affected by outliers, and which much less so?
cards.answer: p = ∞ is very affected by outliers, while p = 1 is much less so.
distractors: p = 1 is very affected by outliers, while p = ∞ is much less so.
p = 2 is the only one affected by outliers.
All p-distances are equally affected by outliers.

cards.question: For the test point o* = [0, 0] and o₃ = [−0.1, 0], why do d₁, d₂ and d∞ all give the same distance of 0.1?
cards.answer: The points differ along only one axis, so every p-distance reduces to the absolute difference along that axis.
distractors: Because all p-distances are equal whenever one point is the origin.
Because the distance is below 1, where all norms agree.
Because o₃ is the nearest neighbour of o*.

cards.question: What is d∞(o₂, o₅) for o₂ = [−0.2, 0.3] and o₅ = [−0.3, −0.2]?
cards.answer: 0.5, the larger of the per-attribute differences 0.1 and 0.5.
distractors: 0.6, the sum of the per-attribute differences.
0.1, the smaller of the per-attribute differences.

cards.question: What is the squared Euclidean norm ‖[0, 0] − [−0.2, 0.3]‖²₂?
Why is the statement 'dₚ(o₄, oₖ) > 0.1 for all k ∈ {1, …, 6} and all p ∈ {1, 2, ∞}' false?
cards.answer: Because k = 4 is included, and the distance from o₄ to itself is 0 under any norm.
distractors: Because the ∞-norm distance to every point is below 0.1.
Because the 1-norm and 2-norm always give distances below 0.1 in 2D.
Because distances are only defined between points of different classes.

cards.question: How is the cosine similarity between x and y defined?
cards.answer: cos(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖₂‖y‖₂).
distractors: cos(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − xᵀy).
cos(x, y) = (f₀₀ + f₁₁) / K.
cos(x, y) = ‖x − y‖₂ / (‖x‖₂‖y‖₂).

cards.question: For binary vectors, what do K, f₀₀ and f₁₁ denote?
cards.answer: K is the total number of attributes, f₀₀ the number where both vectors are 0, and f₁₁ the number where both are 1.
distractors: K is the number of neighbours, f₀₀ the number of mismatches, and f₁₁ the number of matches.
K is the number of attributes where the vectors differ, and f₀₀ and f₁₁ are their norms.
K is the number of 1s in x, f₀₀ the number of 0s in y, and f₁₁ the number of 1s in y.

cards.question: What is the difference between the Simple Matching Coefficient and the Jaccard coefficient?
cards.answer: SMC = (f₀₀ + f₁₁)/K counts shared 0s as matches, while Jaccard = f₁₁/(K − f₀₀) ignores attributes where both vectors are 0.
distractors: SMC ignores shared 0s, while Jaccard counts them as matches.
SMC is for continuous vectors, while Jaccard is for binary vectors.
They are always equal for binary vectors.

cards.question: Customer 1 bought [Bread, Soda, Milk, Beer, Diaper] = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0] and customer 2 bought [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]. What are SMC, Jaccard and cosine similarity?
How is the extended Jaccard coefficient defined, and how does it relate to the Jaccard coefficient on binary data?
cards.answer: EJ(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − xᵀy), and it agrees with the Jaccard coefficient when the data is binary.
distractors: EJ(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖₂‖y‖₂), and it equals cosine similarity on binary data.
EJ(x, y) = (f₀₀ + f₁₁)/K, and it equals SMC on binary data.
EJ(x, y) = xᵀy / (‖x‖² + ‖y‖²), and it is always half the Jaccard coefficient.

cards.question: What does it mean for a dissimilarity d to be scale invariant?
cards.answer: d(x, y) = d(αx, y): rescaling one input does not change the measure.
distractors: d(x, y) = d(α + x, y): shifting one input does not change the measure.
d(x, y) = d(y, x): the order of the inputs does not matter.
d(x, x) = 0: an object has zero distance to itself.

cards.question: What does it mean for a dissimilarity d to be translation invariant?
cards.answer: d(x, y) = d(α + x, y): adding a constant offset to one input does not change the measure.
distractors: d(x, y) = d(αx, y): rescaling one input does not change the measure.
d(x, y) = d(y, x): the order of the inputs does not matter.
d(x, y) is unchanged when attributes are reordered.

cards.question: Persons x, y and z have (children, age, salary) = (0, 44, 45000), (0, 44, 50000) and (2, 44, 50000). Why is d₂(x, y) much larger than d₂(y, z), and what fixes this?
cards.answer: Salary has a far larger scale and dominates the Euclidean distance; standardizing each attribute prevents one attribute from dominating.
distractors: Number of children is a ratio attribute and must be removed; one-out-of-K encoding fixes this.
Age is identical for all three, which inflates the distance; removing age fixes this.
Euclidean distance is scale invariant, so the result is correct and needs no fix.

cards.question: When combining heterogeneous attributes, age similarity is defined as s_Age = a / (a + d₁(x_Age, y_Age)) with a = 1. What is s_Age when two people's ages differ by 1 year?
How are a binary education similarity and a continuous age similarity combined into one overall similarity?
cards.answer: Compute s_Edu with SMC and s_Age from a transformed distance, then combine them, for example as the average ½(s_Edu + s_Age) or a weighted sum.
distractors: Compute one Euclidean distance over the raw education and age attributes together.
Use only the attribute with the largest scale.
Multiply the raw age by the number of education levels.

cards.question: What does the weighted similarity s(x, y) = 0.99 s_Edu + 0.01 s_Age express?
cards.answer: That education is considered far more important than age when comparing objects.
distractors: That age is considered far more important than education.
That the two attributes have been standardized to equal importance.
That 99% of the objects have education data and 1% have age data.

cards.question: How does the squared Mahalanobis distance differ from the squared Euclidean distance?
cards.answer: It replaces the identity matrix with the inverse covariance matrix: (x − y)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − y).
distractors: It replaces the identity matrix with the covariance matrix itself: (x − y)ᵀ Σ (x − y).
It takes the maximum absolute difference instead of the sum of squares.
It divides the Euclidean distance by the number of attributes.

cards.question: Under the Mahalanobis distance, what happens to distances along directions where the data has high variance?
cards.answer: Moving along high-variance directions counts as a shorter distance.
distractors: Moving along high-variance directions counts as a longer distance.
High-variance directions are ignored completely.
Distances are the same in every direction, as with the Euclidean distance.

cards.question: In very high dimensions, what happens to the ratio between the smallest and largest Euclidean distances among random points?
cards.answer: It approaches 1, so all points become nearly equidistant from each other.
distractors: It approaches 0, so nearest neighbours become extremely close.
It grows without bound.
It stays the same as in low dimensions.

cards.question: How does the number of points needed to densely cover a unit hypercube grow with the dimension?
cards.answer: Exponentially, even though the cube's volume stays 1.
distractors: Linearly, in proportion to the dimension.
It stays the same, since the volume is always 1.
It decreases, since the points spread out.

cards.question: In a 20-dimensional box filled with random points, what is surprising about a given point's surroundings?
cards.answer: In high enough dimension, the boundaries of the box are closer to it than any other point in the box.
distractors: Its nearest neighbour is always at distance 0.
All other points lie closer to it than the boundaries do.
It always lies at the exact centre of the box.

cards.question: What are the three components of supervised learning?
cards.answer: Data (inputs and outputs), a model f(x; w) with parameters w, and a cost function d(y, f(x; w)) measuring the dissimilarity between observation and prediction.
distractors: Data (inputs only), a similarity measure, and a set of clusters.
A model, a decoder, and a latent representation.
A confusion matrix, an error rate, and a test point.

cards.question: In supervised learning, what role does the cost function play?
cards.answer: It measures the dissimilarity between the observed output and the model's prediction, telling us whether the model is good or bad.
distractors: It is the function with parameters w that maps inputs to outputs.
It lists the inputs and outputs we are given.
It decides how many neighbours to use.

cards.question: What are the steps of the K-nearest neighbour classifier, once K and a distance measure are chosen?
cards.answer: Compute the distance to all other data objects, find the K nearest, and classify by majority vote among them.
distractors: Compute the class means, then assign the class whose mean is nearest.
Find the K nearest objects, then predict the average of their output values.
Fit a model with parameters w, then classify using its output.

cards.question: Training data (height, weight): males (183, 90), (180, 75), (170, 85), (185, 83); females (159, 59), (167, 75), (165, 68), (175, 72). With Euclidean distance and K = 1, how is the new point (171, 82) classified?
cards.answer: Male, because its single nearest neighbour is the male at (170, 85).
distractors: Female, because its nearest neighbour is the female at (167, 75).
Female, because there are more females nearby than males.
It cannot be classified with K = 1.

cards.question: For the same data, with Euclidean distance and K = 3, how is (171, 82) classified?
cards.answer: Female, because its three nearest neighbours are the male at (170, 85) and the females at (167, 75) and (175, 72).
distractors: Male, because its nearest neighbour is male.
Male, because two of its three nearest neighbours are male.
It is a tie that must be broken randomly.

cards.question: Why can K = 2 or K = 4 cause problems in a two-class K-nearest neighbour classifier?
cards.answer: An even K can produce a tie (for example 1/2 votes for each class), so a tie-breaking rule is needed.
distractors: An even K always makes the classifier predict the majority class in the whole dataset.
An even K makes the distance computation undefined.
An even K is equivalent to K = 1.

cards.question: In a KNN decision-boundary quiz, plot C has a boundary passing exactly between every pair of neighbouring points of different classes. Which K does it correspond to?
distractors: K = 3 with ties broken by the second nearest neighbour.

cards.question: For a K = 3 classifier on three classes, what tie-breaking rule did the correct decision boundary in the quiz assume?
cards.answer: Assign the point to the class of its nearest neighbour.
distractors: Assign the point to the class of its second nearest neighbour.
Assign the point to a random class among the tied ones.
Assign the point to the largest class in the training set.

cards.question: A confusion matrix shows 4 mammals predicted as mammals, 2 mammals predicted as non-mammals, 1 non-mammal predicted as mammal, and 8 non-mammals predicted correctly. What are the accuracy and error rate?
cards.answer: Accuracy = 12/15 = 0.8, error rate = 3/15 = 0.2.
distractors: Accuracy = 4/6 ≈ 0.67, error rate ≈ 0.33.
Accuracy = 8/9 ≈ 0.89, error rate ≈ 0.11.
Accuracy = 0.2, error rate = 0.8.

cards.question: How are accuracy and error rate related?
cards.answer: They sum to 1: accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions, and error rate is the fraction of incorrect ones.
distractors: The error rate is the square of 1 minus the accuracy.
Accuracy is the number of correct predictions, and error rate is the number of incorrect predictions in the largest class.
They are independent and can both be high at the same time.

cards.question: What does a confusion matrix show?
cards.answer: The counts of actual versus predicted class labels.
distractors: The covariance between each pair of attributes.
The distances between each pair of data objects.
The decision boundaries for different values of K.

cards.question: How does KNN regression predict the output for a test observation x?
cards.answer: It predicts the average y-value of the K nearest training points: ŷ = (1/K) Σ yᵢ over the neighbourhood.
distractors: It predicts the most common y-value among the K nearest training points.
It predicts the y-value of the farthest training point.
It fits a straight line through all training points.

cards.question: Why is the KNN regression prediction piecewise constant, as seen for K = 1?
cards.answer: Over an interval of inputs, the set of nearest neighbours stays the same, so their average prediction does not change.
distractors: Because KNN regression rounds every prediction to the nearest integer.
Because KNN regression only predicts values seen at the test points.
Because the distance measure is the max-norm.

cards.question: What is the difference between descriptive and predictive regression modelling?
cards.answer: Descriptive modelling explains the relation between attributes and a continuous output; predictive modelling predicts the output value of a new data object.
distractors: Descriptive modelling predicts outputs for new objects; predictive modelling explains relationships.
Descriptive modelling has discrete outputs; predictive modelling has continuous outputs.
Descriptive modelling uses KNN; predictive modelling uses regression trees.

cards.question: How is a regression model evaluated?
cards.answer: By the average loss per observation, E = (1/N) Σ L(yᵢ, f(xᵢ)), using L₁ = |y − ŷ| or L₂ = (y − ŷ)².
distractors: By the accuracy, the fraction of exactly correct predictions.
By the confusion matrix of actual versus predicted values.
By the correlation between the inputs.

cards.question: What does the L₂ loss for regression compute?
cards.answer: The squared difference (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² between the observation and the prediction.
distractors: The absolute difference |yᵢ − ŷᵢ|.
The maximum difference over all observations.
1 if the prediction is wrong, 0 if it is right.

cards.question: In the teaser for evaluating KNN on unseen data, how is each observation xᵢ evaluated?
cards.answer: Remove xᵢ from the data, classify it using its neighbours among the remaining points, record whether it was correct, and repeat for all N points.
distractors: Classify xᵢ using all data including itself, so it is always its own nearest neighbour.
Classify only the first point and assume the rest behave the same.
Compute the distance from xᵢ to the class means and repeat once.

cards.question: Which questions about KNN methods were left open for later in the course?
cards.answer: How to systematically select K and the distance measure, and how to properly evaluate on unseen data.
distractors: How to compute Euclidean distances and majority votes.
How to compute the median of the training data.
How to store data points as rows of a matrix.
